The Most Comfortable Sneakers for Women, Tested by a Style Writer

📅 29 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • At this point, I’m pretty sure I qualify as the woman who lived in her shoes.
  • So, I present to you the pairs of comfortable shoes—think walking shoes and cross-training shoes—that actually keep me feeling comfortable and supported without slacking on cuteness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

At this point, I’m pretty sure I qualify as the woman who lived in her shoes. Not in a glamorous Carrie Bradshaw kind of way, but in a professional-sneaker-tester kind of way. I probs have at least 30 pairs crowding my closet and entryways right now, and that’s not even counting the pairs I’ve run into the ground or given away to friends and family (you’re welcome). My top priority is always comfort, and while you might find that a given when it comes to sneakers, I’ve tested my fair share of options that make my feet feel stiff and achy.

So, I present to you the pairs of comfortable shoes—think walking shoes and cross-training shoes—that actually keep me feeling comfortable and supported without slacking on cuteness. From memory foam insoles that mold to your foot's unique shape to running shoes with responsive soles that absorb your stride’s shock, these are the most comfortable sneakers for women, tested by myself and other sneaker enthusiasts at Women’s Health.

Recent findings suggest that the brand ethos of On is to make people feel like they're running on Clouds. It achieves this thanks to its signature Helion Superfoam midsole, which sets itself apart with a construction that blends rigid, stable sections with flexible foam. This combination of materials provides the perfect balance of cushioning and energy return, giving you a bouncy, lightweight feel when your foot hits the pavement. The result is a soft, natural ground feel, rather than an overly bouncy cushioning experience. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi notes this tech alone is why this shoe is an absolute workhorse when it comes to running (and running fast!). It’s her all-time favorite race shoe—she even ran a half-marathon in it.

Recent findings suggest that according to Accardi, the shoe feels firm but still has enough flexibility that her running gait isn’t impacted. The toebox has a ton of room for movement, but still holds the foot in place so each step feels responsive and energetic. Even when her legs feel like they’re about to give out, these shoes pick her right back up. On’s innovative speedboard, a flexible plastic plate wedged between the footbed and midsole, snaps back into place for a bouncy effect after your feet hit the ground. This means the shoe requires less energy output with each stride, making running feel easier. Plus, the rebound that comes with the underfoot cushioning gives a spring in your step.

I might not run marathons like Accardi, but I love to wear this shoe for walking and casual jogs. The CloudTec system, which uses air pockets in the midsole (the layer between the insole and the outsole), to create the shoe’s cushiony feel, propels me forward with every step, kind of like walking on a trampoline. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy T-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

According to recent reports, one thing to note, though, is the sole wears down fast, which we found to be disappointing, especially given that price tag. Accardi says the Clifton 10 has a better tread thanks to its thicker outsole designed for high-friction.

Read more: On Cloudmonster 3 Review.

Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!). That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it literally feels like walking on pillows.

With the most cushioning of any shoe on this list (and the most cushioning Brooks offers), it’s perfect for those who need extra support. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton notes it has extra plush, foamy cushioning, but even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s incredibly stable thanks to Brooks’ signature Guardrails technology, which is a broad base with two pieces of foam on either side of the heel. It reduces the rolling of the foot both inward and outward, so it cradles your foot in place without messing with your stride. According to Appleton, this combination is great for those with higher arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel an ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options (huge win!).

During testing, I did notice that there was some wear and tear on the shoe pretty early on (it had only been a few months of use). The material on the upper of the shoe wore out pretty promptly. While this knocked it down a few points in my book, its supreme comfort still kept this kick at the very top of my list. Plus, I love how many fun colors the shoe comes in—because running and walking should be fun, right?!

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

According to recent reports, the Hoka Clifton 11 is a standout favorite among WH editors. After testing nearly every Hoka model, I can attest that the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar—just a smidge lighter and more springy. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning.

The first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly narrower, too, but it doesn’t feel tight or uncomfortable. I prefer the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Sources indicate that despite its lighter weight, it has a generous stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also find that the foam absorbs impact well. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never feel fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride feels smooth and natural whether I’m walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the newly introduced Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

There’s nothing worse than slipping into an uncomfortable shoe after a tough run—that’s where the Alo Recovery Sneaker comes in. Designed to support tired feet, it features a structured sole and high-rebound foam insole that offers arch support and bounces back into place with each step. It makes every step feel stable, cushioned, and balanced. The second I put this pair on after a long run, my feet are instantly relaxed. I can’t say that about most of my other sneakers.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest perks of this shoe? The traction is next-level, which is key for a recovery sneaker that’s meant to keep you comfortable and steady all day. Inside, the sock-like lining prevents your foot from sliding around. The thick ankle collar also helps stabilize the foot and provides extra support up the leg, keeping everything locked in place.

Style-wise, this sneaker goes with everything—sweats, shorts, jeans, leggings, you name it. That’s why I crowned it the best overall platform sneaker. After giving it a spin for a few weeks running around Manhattan, walking my dog around Long Island, and wearing it to and from workout classes, it's done the best job at keeping my feet pain-free compared to many other platform sneakers I've worn. The 1.5-inch platform is subtle but adds just the right amount of height to elongate my legs without being so tall that I feel unstable. Oh, and it’s super cute to boot. I’m a major fan of the Natural White colorway, which looks clean and classic, and pairs effortlessly with everything from sweatpants to denim.

Even if you’re not fresh off a run, it works for the office, errands, or a casual lunch. It’s hands down one of the most versatile (and most worn) shoes in my closet. My one con is that it feels a bit heavy and bulky, especially after a long day of wear.

Read more: Alo Recovery Mode Sneaker Review.

According to recent reports, I hadn't tried Asics until this year, and now it's my go-to shoe brand. Not only does its shoe have a streetwear vibe (I'm loving the bright yellow color with sweats and jeans), but they’re also some of the most comfortable shoes I’ve ever worn. In the UB9-S Gel Kayano 20s, the brand uses its signature gel cushioning technology, which features gel units placed in both the heel and forefoot of the shoe to absorb shock and provide a soft landing. This cushioning adapts to your foot’s movement, offering flexibility while reducing impact on your joints. Plus, the form-fitting upper keeps your foot locked in place, making it perfect for long runs, but stylish enough for everyday wear.

Recent findings suggest that I wear this shoe everywhere—on runs, in the gym, and even to the office—and I get compliments virtually every single time I step out in it. The support is unmatched, the traction is solid, and it’s lightweight enough that I never feel weighed down. Plus, it breaks in fast (I wore it right out of the box), so there’s no awkward adjustment period. If you’re looking for a sneaker that can do it all while still looking cool, this is the one for you.

It has been revealed that one con to note: It comes in some funky colors, so if you’re not into something bright and fun, I’d recommend looking elsewhere. I also wish it came in a wider version for those with wider feet and bunions.

Read More: Asics Gel-Kayano 20 Review.

It has been revealed that we’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” says WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

Now with a lighter weight and a lower heel-to-toe drop (6 mm compared to 9.5 mm), the shoe doesn’t weigh me down and puts less stress on the ankles and feet. I’m a significant fan of the wider base for lifting and squatting because it makes my feet feel locked. The forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter add extra security, while the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

It has been revealed that and post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. I recently wore this sneaker while traveling, and it kept my feet happy power walking through the airport and standing in long security and customs lines. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

The fit is true to size, and while wide-size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, the wide outsole may feel too bulky during stair climbing or quick, dynamic moves.

Read More: lululemon Chargefeel 3 Review.

Sources indicate that let me introduce you to my fresh favorite low-profile, fashion sneaker: the Puma Speedcat. It’s been making waves with style girls, and after testing it out for months, I can see why. This shoe pairs so well with any outfit, with a slim, almost ballet-flat silhouette that doesn’t clash with nicer pieces in my wardrobe. I even see celebs like Em Rata sport the Speedcat all the time, and they always make any streetwear ‘fit look so chic and cool.

Like the Samba, it has a pretty flat sole, but I actually find it more cushioned thanks to its EVA midsole, which has a lightweight, cushioned feel and shock-absorbing properties. This means I can walk around for longer without my feet aching. Plus, after wearing it on wet city streets, I’ve noticed it has better traction, which is a huge win.

It has been revealed that the only downside? The fit is a little narrow, especially in the toe area. If you have wider feet, I’d definitely recommend sizing up.

Read More: Puma Speedcat OG Review.

Recent findings suggest that originally designed for indoor soccer, the Adidas Samba has become a cult-favorite sneaker that’s just as popular on the streets as it is on the field. At first glance, the Samba looks pretty flat, so I wasn’t expecting much in terms of comfort. But after logging hundreds of miles walking around the city, I was surprised by how well it supports my feet. The Samba uses a combination of synthetic leather for the upper and a rubber sole with a cushioned midsole for comfort. The cushioning is more subtle compared to high-performance running shoes, but it still provides a soft, supportive feel. Even without a ton of cushioning, I rarely experience discomfort, which is impressive for a sneaker this sleek. It runs narrow, especially for wide feet, and I recommend going a half size down, as it tends to run major—many with wider feet or bunions agree it’s not the best fit.

In a recent development, it’s a go-to for effortlessly cool outfits—you can wear it with jeans, dresses, slacks, or shorts and always look stylish. I own this shoe in two different colorways (it comes in so many different shades), and after wearing it with practically everything in my closet, I can confidently say it adds a sporty, trendy touch to any outfit.

One of Under Armour’s first-ever shoes, this kick is rooted in sport. But it’s gotten some essential upgrades since its launch, and it’s safe to say I’m hooked. Since 2009, it’s been updated with leather upper overlays to keep the foot supported and soft UA HOVR cushioning, made from soft EVA foam and rubber, which is engineered to store and release energy with each step, providing a bouncy, responsive feel that helps propel you forward. Out of all the shoes I’ve tried, this pair feels the most bouncy, which I know is an absolute essential for the runners and walkers out there that like that super thick underfoot feel. It also has a rocker shape to keep the foot in a forward motion for less energy exertion.

The UA Apparition also has a mesh upper for supreme breathability—I’ve worn it during HIIT workouts, runs, and walks and never feel like my feet are constricted or sweaty, but I still feel supported and balanced. With a sleek, minimalistic look, the Apparition pairs well with anything from gym gear to casual streetwear. The rubber outsole provides traction and durability, allowing for smooth transitions during both dynamic workouts and everyday use.

In a recent development, my one con? There are some fun colors available, but I wish there were more options to choose from.

According to recent reports, when it comes to comfortable sneakers, cushioning should be your top priority—whether you’re walking, running, hitting the gym, or just running errands. Here are the cushioning levels you can expect to see in the shoes below:.

As Women’s Health editors, we practically live in sneakers, so we know what it takes for a shoe to feel super comfortable. When I originally put together this list of the most comfortable sneakers in 2025, I spent over two years testing more than 50 pairs in every possible scenario—long and short walks, runs, HIIT workouts, full days out in NYC, travel days, and more. For this 2026 enhancement, myself and other WH editors re-tested newer iterations of our favorite pairs to make sure they still meet our standards. I also sought advice from fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, as well as style contributor Lily Wohlner. We looked at everything from cushioning and stability to sizing, traction, and color options. And if a pair left our feet aching or uncomfortable, it didn’t make the cut. So you can trust that every sneaker on this list kept our feet happy all day long—even through our toughest workouts.

Morpho’s largest euro stablecoin vault is €13.8 million short of covering its biggest depositor’s exit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that morpho’s largest listed vault for EUR CoinVertible (EURCV), a euro stablecoin, highlighted about 13.8 million EURCV less liquidity than its biggest address would need for a full exit on Nov.
  • A withdrawal would return EURCV to a wallet, but eligible holders seeking euros directly from issuer SG-FORGE would follow a separate redemption timetable.
  • Morpho’s Steakhouse Prime EURCV vault on Ethereum showed 144.3 million EURCV in deposits and 107.2 million in displayed liquidity, including tokens the app could pull from other lending markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that morpho’s largest listed vault for EUR CoinVertible (EURCV), a euro stablecoin, highlighted about 13.8 million EURCV less liquidity than its biggest address would need for a full exit on Nov. 26.

A withdrawal would return EURCV to a wallet, but eligible holders seeking euros directly from issuer SG-FORGE would follow a separate redemption timetable.

Morpho’s Steakhouse Prime EURCV vault on Ethereum showed 144.3 million EURCV in deposits and 107.2 million in displayed liquidity, including tokens the app could pull from other lending markets.

The top address accounted for 121 million EURCV (83.8%), according to the same page. Steakhouse Prime was the largest EURCV vault by assets in Morpho’s public ranking.

The comparison assumes the top address sought to withdraw its entire position at that moment. Morpho’s public data show balances by address, which can pool funds for more than one owner.

The European Banking Authority’s Nov. 25 report on stablecoins in decentralized finance found that, in its July analysis, more than half of circulating EURCV was supplied to a Morpho vault.

Sources indicate that A standard vault withdrawal draws on idle tokens and funds that can be pulled from the market designated for withdrawals. At Ethereum block 26,500,641, Morpho’s address-level position data put that route’s limit at 103.1 million EURCV against a position worth 120.99 million.

That left about 17.9 million EURCV beyond the ordinary withdrawal limit at the indexed block.

Under Morpho’s withdrawal rules, the app can pull available funds from other markets when the vault configuration allows it, a process called forced deallocation.

Morpho’s withdrawal-options data demonstrated about 102.8 million EURCV idle and about $340,000 available in the designated market, plus about 4 million that could be pulled from other markets, based on rounded amounts.

Industry observers note that that last source of funds explains why the app highlighted more liquidity than a standard withdrawal could use. What a depositor can withdraw depends on what is still available when the transaction executes.

In a lending market where borrowers are using most of the funds, repayments or fresh deposits can free up tokens for another withdrawal.

On eligible vaults, Morpho also offers an in-kind exit that can return some EURCV to the wallet and convert part of the redeemed amount into a direct position in a lending market.

According to recent reports, two Nov. 26 liquidity readings show how much of the largest position the vault could cover in a hypothetical full exit.

Vault liquidity controls how many tokens can leave. Direct issuer redemption has its own eligibility checks and cash deadline.

China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong.
  • The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.
  • The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

Sources indicate that the CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

In a recent development, the program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

According to recent reports, the obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

Industry observers note that CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and noted it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither organization has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

Recent findings suggest that COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, Newly introduced York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

In a recent development, for years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Recent findings suggest that now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

Recent findings suggest that and this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.
  • In a recent development, chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

In a recent development, chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”.

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the massive bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

According to recent reports, “Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”.

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is at the moment operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The substantial trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

Industry observers note that “The midweight material is a bit thicker, so it smoothes better than many other styles,” Nied states. “Still, they feel more like pajamas than activewear, and I honestly find myself wearing them to sleep more than workouts,” Nied says. “But don’t get me wrong, they can keep up with a workout just as well.” That’s because the elastane blend offers insane stretch and moisture-wicking capabilities that keep up with any sweat sesh. Zoller adds that she never feels the need to tug at them or adjust mid-pose.

“When you’re shopping for yoga pants, you want more than just a cute pair—you want leggings that actually work for your practice,” states Melody Zoller, NASM, a personal trainer and senior director at obé Fitness. “The right pair should feel good against your skin, move with you through every twist, fold, and lunge, and give you the level of support you need without constant tugging or adjusting.” She recommends looking for blends of the following materials:.

It has been revealed that all the options on this list are high-rise. Why? During yoga, you need something that stays up, holds your stomach in, and covers your midriff, especially during twisting and upside-down poses, Zoller indicates. A high-rise pair will help keep your lower body locked in while bending and changing positions. Opt for a slim or tapered cut to prevent extra fabric from bunching up during certain poses. That’s not to say a flare can’t work (especially for a more chill practice or day-to-day wear), but a slimmer hem or bootcut is more functional.

Look for a light to medium level of compression for your yoga pants, Zoller says.   • And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie revealed the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”.

In a recent development, greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” remarked Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”.

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The organization says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

HRF Announces Funding of Seven Bitcoin Projects for People Living Under Authoritarian Regimes

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) is pleased to announce grants from its Bitcoin Development Fund for seven projects advancing bitcoin self-custody, financial privacy, and education for people living under authoritarian regimes.
  • One project translates bitcoin terminology into 21 African languages.
  • Together, these efforts help human rights defenders, journalists, nonprofits, and individuals hold, send, and verify their money freely under repression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Human Rights Foundation (HRF) is pleased to announce grants from its Bitcoin Development Fund for seven projects advancing bitcoin self-custody, financial privacy, and education for people living under authoritarian regimes.

One project translates bitcoin terminology into 21 African languages. Another mines bitcoin with surplus solar power in rural Nigerian homes, paying it directly to the households that generate it. Others build tools for people facing repression anywhere — activists who need to find and fix the privacy leaks in their bitcoin use, communities who need self-custody devices built from parts found in any electronics store, observers who need election evidence preserved before it disappears, and people who need to turn an ordinary phone into an offline Bitcoin wallet.

Together, these efforts help human rights defenders, journalists, nonprofits, and individuals hold, send, and verify their money freely under repression.

HRF’s grantees for Round III of 2026 are:.

According to recent reports, many people want to self-custody bitcoin, but in much of the world, buying a hardware wallet is too expensive. CryoBrick transforms feature phones into offline Bitcoin signing devices. Because it looks and works like an ordinary phone, activists living under authoritarian regimes can self-custody bitcoin while maintaining plausible deniability. Technical Director Apalok will use HRF’s support to conduct comprehensive security hardening and peer review, integrate Bitchat for offline messaging, and publish how-to guides, expanding access to bitcoin and the property rights it protects to a far larger global user base.

According to recent reports, bitcoin’s benefits remain out of reach for many African communities because high-quality education resources do not exist in their local languages. Exonumia, an open-source project that translates Bitcoin educational content, is building a Bitcoin Glossary in 21 African languages. The project will coordinate a continent-wide community of translators through three in-person and 12 virtual translation sprints, where native speakers review and validate more than 250 terms. Because every term is validated by native speakers rather than machines, the approved terms give wallet developers a trustworthy foundation for localizing bitcoin software into African languages, extending access to bitcoin education and the financial freedom it offers. HRF’s support will see the glossary published as a free public resource.

Recent findings suggest that in much of Africa, democratic elections remain a struggle and most countries are not fully free. Exacerbating this, evidence of fraud documented by citizens is often lost because paper forms go missing and photos and messages cannot be verified. Pawavox, created by Nigerian civic-tech founder Jason Omu, is a platform that gives election observers and human rights defenders a upcoming way to record irregularities. Using Pawavox, observers capture short video or voice reports, each GPS-tagged and timestamped. This evidence is then published to Nostr, a decentralized communications protocol, as a record that is much harder for anyone to tamper with. HRF’s grant will help fund the completion of the Nostr integration and expansion across Africa, helping protect the integrity of the evidence on which democratic accountability depends.

Industry observers note that branded hardware wallets are a common way to self-custody bitcoin, but under repressive regimes, they can be expensive and attract unwanted attention. SeedSigner is an open-source signing device that consumers assemble themselves from inexpensive, widely available parts, so there is no finished-device supply chain for an attacker to compromise. It right now runs on a small computer, called a Raspberry Pi Zero, which can be unavailable in regions that need self-custody most. Lead maintainer Keith Mukai will use HRF’s support to migrate the SeedSigner code to more widely available hardware, ending dependence on any single manufacturer. Then, more individuals under repressive regimes will be able to hold their own bitcoin without trusting anyone else.

Many people assume they gain financial privacy by using bitcoin, but bitcoin is a public network, and the ways they compromise their privacy are often invisible. Stealth is an open-source auditing tool that runs directly on a user’s node (a computer that verifies the Bitcoin network). It analyzes a bitcoin wallet using the same techniques that blockchain analytics firms employ, then produces a report with severity levels, confidence scores, and concrete fixes for users. The HRF grant supports lead maintainer LORDBABUINO in adding support for the main Bitcoin network and building packages for standard node kits. With this tool, activists will be able to better spot the privacy leaks they leave behind when using Bitcoin, before an adversary does.

Nigeria is one of the world’s most active digital asset markets, but the legal path to acquiring bitcoin runs through exchanges that collect troves of identity and transactional data. At the same time, many rural Nigerian homes are receiving solar electricity for the first time, but much of that power goes unused in the daytime. Strandedwatt, a bitcoin mining initiative, installs small open-source Bitcoin miners in homes, converting surplus solar power into bitcoin, which is paid privately and directly to host households. The next step, backed by HRF, will see Bitnob CEO and project lead Bernard Parah deploy 100 Jua Kali miners in these homes and publish an open-source playbook other communities can replicate. Meanwhile, households excluded by the Nigerian financial system gain a permissionless path to freedom money.

Industry observers note that A commercial Bitcoin hardware wallet has software and hardware the user cannot inspect, and carrying one can signal to outsiders that someone owns bitcoin. Specter DIY is a fully open-source, air-gapped Bitcoin hardware wallet that anyone can build from off-the-shelf components and verify line by line. There is no purchase record, and the finished device does not look like a Bitcoin wallet at all. For activists in Belarus, dissidents in Venezuela, and journalists in Burma, it is a path to financial self-sovereignty. HRF’s grant to the Specter Association, the nonprofit that maintains the project, helps fund hardware costs, AI tooling, and vulnerability bounties, ensuring the developers behind a self-custody tool dissidents can inspect and verify remain supported.

Tech Report: Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.
  • Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.
  • Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Recent findings suggest that musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”.

It has been revealed that on Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

As we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 proposal, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Industry observers note that brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

Recent findings suggest that the memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c.

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:.

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:.

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”.

Recent findings suggest that that’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself claims is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

According to recent reports, this Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

According to recent reports, besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

It has been revealed that what do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that since I was old enough to record playlists on cassette tapes, I’ve paired music with my intense crushes. Each guy basically had his own song, sometimes an entire soundtrack.

According to recent reports, I fell in love with my college boyfriend to the tune of Bruce Springsteen’s “Dancing in the Dark,” while Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue was the anthem that played throughout a 15-year situationship with an elusive artist. Then, there was the whirlwind romance with a former smoke jumper turned ER doctor whose last concert was Emmylou Harris, which reminded me of the then-popular song “Emmylou” by First Aid Kit.

Each time, I became as obsessed with the song as the guy associated with it. My brain hyperfixated on the lyrics, first looking for hopeful clues, and then after the romance ended, sparking memories of sweet moments.

According to recent reports, music is often seen as a source of comfort for those dealing with heartbreak, but it can actually “arouse feelings of romantic longing, particularly searing melody,” states Walter Frisch, PhD, a professor of music at Columbia University. Some composers call such a haunting melody “l’idée fixe” or “fixed idea.”.

Once that “fixed idea” gets stuck in your head—in the form of a song played on repeat—it can actually trigger the thoughts that land you in limerence, the involuntarily obsessive rumination on an idealized love interest. It’s fueled by both the hope that the person you like likes you back and the uncertainty of whether they do.

For a long time, I thought I was alone in my lyric-fueled limerence, but as I interviewed experts and other limerents as research for my memoir, When Longing Becomes Your Lover, I learned that it’s incredibly common—and normal—for our brains to connect music with unrequited lovers.

Industry observers note that neuroscience would call this melody intermittent reinforcement. When we are infatuated with someone, we are anticipating connection with that person, which results in our brain’s reward system releasing the “feel good” hormone dopamine. As a result, we are motivated to return to the behavior of deeply thinking, or ruminating, about them to get that reward.

Sources indicate that in one famous MRI brain scan study, when heartbroken individuals were shown pictures of their heartbreakers, their dopamine pathways lit up just as they would from doing cocaine. Similarly, music can trigger someone to ruminate about what could be or what could have been with a romantic interest, indicates psychiatrist Jud Brewer, MD, PhD, the director of research and innovation at Brown University’s Mindfulness Center and author of The Craving Mind. The result, he says, is an itchy, contracted, restless feeling—quite the opposite of the expansive feeling associated with the mindfulness used to stop craving and anxiety.

Nostalgia also triggers the release of dopamine, and a song is like a time machine. Anytime I hear “Dancing in the Dark,” I’m instantly transported to kissing my college boyfriend in a dark, musty stairwell off campus. I can feel his hands resting on my hips and taste the Kentucky bourbon on his lips.

“There’s this certain charge you can get remembering somebody that you've been with before,” says Geoff MacDonald, PhD, a social psychologist who studies singlehood and sexuality at the University of Toronto. “You can replay, sort of viscerally, what it felt like to have somebody who was into you [and] that has the potential to provide real validation.”.

Industry observers note that he points to one study on song lyrics and attachment styles that, he says, “provides some evidence that people are drawn to a self-reinforcing bubble when it comes to intimacy.” In other words, it’s a form of confirmation bias. You’re drawn to songs with lyrics that reinforce what you already think about relationships, and you’re more likely to read into those lyrics and apply them to your own life.

In a recent development, for example, if you have an anxious attachment style—which many limerents do—you typically feel insecure in relationships and fear abandonment. Consequently, you may need constant validation, which is exactly what a certain song can provide. When I heard “Emmylou” playing on the radio one morning after the sexy smoke jumper had grown more distant over text, I decided it was a sign from the universe that we were still meant to be together. (It wasn’t.).

So, what’s a forlorn lover to do? Purge your playlist. “When someone is addicted to a behavior, if they avoid the people, places, and things [associated with the behavior], they’re less likely to get triggered to do the behavior,” indicates Brewer. “It’s not a great long-term solution, but it's one step that they can take.”.

Sources indicate that think of songs that trigger you to ruminate, whether you’re obsessing over a crush or languishing over a lost love. Maybe it’s a song whose lyrics remind you of them, or a tune you danced to together. Whatever it is, consider removing that song from your playlist—at least until hearing the first few notes no longer launches you into a two-hour daydream about your love interest.

According to recent reports, now, if you've got a playlist that you play once every couple of weeks when you're feeling lonely, that can probably stay in your Spotify rotation. “It's good to remember that you can be loved,” MacDonald notes. “But if you're leaning into that as a replacement for actually seeking real intimacy in your life, that's where you're going to run into problems.”.

Industry observers note that instead of relying on songs to dream about relationships that would never materialize, I deliberately poured that relentless energy into hobbies that gave my life purpose. That might look like spending quality time with a loved one, creating art, or planning a trip—anything that takes your mind off the individual and fills your self-worth bucket.

Now, I can listen to Kind of Blue and “Emmylou” without yearning for past lovers, but I prefer playing songs that reinforce the security I feel in my marriage, like “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” the song we walked down the aisle to.

Amanda McCracken is a journalist, writing professor at the University of Colorado, the author of When Longing Becomes Your Lover, and the host of The Longing Lab podcast.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the U.S. Justice Department said Tuesday that its largest-ever crackdown on scammers has produced actions against more than 800 defendants since March, with cryptocurrency investment fraud run out of Southeast Asian scam centers among its top targets.

The department confirmed the results of an anti-scam surge that followed President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14390, signed March 6. Since then, prosecutors have acted in more than 400 cases, bringing latest charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts and sentences across 85 federal districts.

It has been revealed that U.S. agents also helped police in more than 10 countries raid foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans. Thirty defendants were extradited to face charges in U.S. courts.

Sources indicate that “Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said. “The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning.”.

In a recent development, crypto sits at the center of much of the effort. The State Department said the U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement it funds and trains have helped freeze more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency and take down more than 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts.

In a recent development, the Justice Department’s Scam Center Strike Force, formed in 2025 to go after Southeast Asian crypto fraud, says its crypto seizure team has restrained about $1.08 billion in cryptocurrency from these schemes. The team is focused on returning stolen funds to victims.

The FBI’s Operation Blackout has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices and helped dismantle more than 29 scam compounds across Asia, Africa and the Middle East, the department remarked. The FBI also helped free and repatriate more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to run scams inside those compounds.

“The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you,” FBI Director Kash Patel stated.

Industry observers note that in the past month alone, the Criminal Division filed or unsealed charges against more than 30 scam defendants, including those tied to Southeast Asian scam centers running crypto investment fraud schemes. Other cases involved inheritance fraud, jury duty imposters working from Georgia prisons and sweepstakes schemes aimed at elderly Americans.

Industry observers note that the Secret Service stated it has restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds during the surge. One of its cases identified a crypto investment conspiracy run from scam centers in Cambodia that targeted at least 174 U.S. victims. In October, a Chinese national was extradited from the Netherlands and arraigned in California over his alleged role.

In a recent development, in Moldova, State Department-backed raids in October shut down five call centers and led to the detention of eight suspected coordinators who allegedly ran fake crypto trading platforms. The SEC remarked that in the last year it charged three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs with defrauding retail investors of more than $14 million.

Homeland Security Investigations stated its fraud cases have led to the seizure or freezing of more than $120 million, including funds held in bank and cryptocurrency accounts.

Sources indicate that the crackdown builds on months of pressure on overseas fraud rings. Trump planned to highlight the push against overseas crypto scams in October, and the U.S. government seized more than $580 million in crypto linked to Southeast Asian scam networks in February. In October 2025, prosecutors moved to seize 127,271 bitcoin tied to a Southeast Asian scam operation.

In a recent development, the stakes are large. Citing Gallup, the department stated 10% of U.S. adults experienced a scam last year, directly or through someone in their household, and Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025, including crypto investment scams.

The department noted that an indictment is merely an allegation and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

#145688. Industry News: Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1493 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • Sources indicate that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators claims Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Sources indicate that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

It has been revealed that then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report states the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

Industry observers note that A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson noted the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

According to recent reports, under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a substantial truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In a recent development, in 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

In a recent development, the NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Industry observers note that our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Sources indicate that three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

It has been revealed that compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Industry observers note that either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

It has been revealed that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

WHEN YOUR HOME gym is short on square footage like mine, you need to carefully think about every piece of equipment before it earns its rightful spot. That’s exactly why kettlebells are a staple in my setup. Over time, I’ve built a small but mighty collection—and every single one gets regular use.

A huge perk of kettlebells is that they don’t hog a lot of space (even in a compact home gym) and are relatively inexpensive, indicates Tyneka Pack, CPT. These are versatile strength-training tools, too, allowing you to get in a full-body workout, along with explosive power movements, says kettlebell specialist Taylor Beebe, CPT.

Recent findings suggest that as with any fitness equipment, improper use of kettlebells can lead to injury. That’s why most trainers, including Beebe, recommend getting coaching on how to use kettlebells before diving in (peep our how to get started with kettlebell exercises guide).

Like dumbbells, kettlebells come in a wide range of weights, materials, and grips, so it’s crucial to determine which type you’re in the market for before you buy.

According to recent reports, after testing a handful of kettlebells, this cast-iron option from Amazon Basics earns its spot at the top of our list because of its budget price tag and versatile weight options. The weight range from 10 to 60 pounds has allowed me to ramp up my training intensity over time.

This kettlebell has consistently been my go-to and favorite even as I’ve expanded my collection. They’re surprisingly sturdy and durable, even after two years of use. WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief also loves this model and has multiple in her home gym, too.

I own it in several weight sizes, and it has a compact shape that’s great for every kettlebell exercise imaginable. The grip is slightly textured and wide enough to do one- or two-handed exercises, but petite enough for smaller hands like mine. I can confidently hold it, even during potential wall-breaking moves like swings, and it’s comfortable to hold, whether I’m doing one set or five.

Recent findings suggest that while these weights have a lot going for them, there is one con: There is no vinyl coating on the bottom (although there is a vinyl version, which WH editors also love). To avoid scratching my floors, I have to set it down carefully or use a mat underneath.

In a recent development, many people prefer a competition-style kettlebell due to its uniform design that’s ideal for high reps and technical moves. The Rep Fitness Adjustable Kettlebell offers a competition-style kettlebell shape with adjustable weights, giving you plenty of space-saving mileage out of one tool.

According to recent reports, this kettlebell is well-designed, stacking five weights in one relatively compact design. (Weight ranges include 8 to 16 kilograms, 16 to 24 kilograms, and 20 to 40 pounds.) To adjust the weight, just push down on the dial with two fingers, twist to your desired weight, and lift. It has a rubber base to protect your floors although—heads up—the rubber coating is only there when you use the kettlebell’s full weight. Otherwise, you’ll want to set down your kettlebell gingerly.

REP’s adjustable kettlebell is made from cast iron and feels durable. The textured handle is easy to grip and has plenty of space for two-handed moves, although it feels slightly wider than others. If space is a premium at your place and you’re looking to grow with your kettlebell, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment.

Industry observers note that if you prefer a more traditional competition-style kettlebell, keep scrolling. But if you’re on the hunt for a highly versatile weight that aims to combine the attributes of a kettlebell with those of a dumbbell and a dual-grip medicine ball, the YBell Neo Series is worth consideration.

This weight is perfect for my needs—it’s relatively compact and offers multiple ways to grip, thanks to its unique pyramid-style design. I can use it for everything from biceps curls to lunges, though it’s not ideal for swings.

According to recent reports, the grip on this is perfection. It features a neoprene outer layer to create a slightly sticky feel with impressive gripping power, so I’m not stressed about accidentally flinging it across the room during swings. The wide handle leaves enough room for one- or two-handed exercises, but it may feel a little crowded using both mitts at once if your hands are on the larger side.

Industry observers note that you have three different spots you can grip on the outside of this weight, along with an inside bar that’s ideal for dumbbell-style work. While the sides are rounded, I found it was relatively easy to rest the YBell on its base or sides to save space.

Sources indicate that the only potential downside of this weight is that it tops out at 26 pounds. If you’re interested in doing heavier lifting, you’ll need to upgrade to a different device.

Industry observers note that A coated kettlebell like this one from Yes4All protects your floors in case of butterfingers through a thoughtfully wrapped coating up the bottom third of the handle. The handle itself makes for a comfortable grip. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says, “I have the 15-pound model and I never feel it slipping away from me when squatting or doing Russian twists.” It comes in five-pound increments up to 65 pounds, giving you plenty of options.

Recent findings suggest that while I wouldn’t recommend tossing this on your floor at home, the kettlebell doesn’t make a loud noise when it’s dropped, unlike uncoated models. It’s also worth pointing out it’s very affordable, similar to our best overall.Just note the bottom of the kettlebell is not entirely flat, which can be tricky if you’re trying exercises like uneven pushups (with one hand placed through the handles of a KB).

Sand kettlebells are a highly portable option that allows you to add a little more instability to your kettlebell workouts. The GoRuck Sand Kettlebell is built tough thanks to its Cordura nylon design and multiple closure system, so you don’t have to stress about accidentally spilling its contents all over the place.

Sources indicate that goRuck’s kettlebell has a teardrop-style shape that works well for many exercises. This kettlebell arrives empty, so you’ll fill it up with sand prior to use. Pro tip: use playground sand available at home improvement stores for this. The reinforcing on nearly all of the seams and bottoms means you can toss this on the ground without worrying about it flying open and spilling sand everywhere.

This style of kettlebell isn’t for everyone, but if you’re looking to add the extra challenge of sandbag training to your kettlebell workouts, this sand kettlebell design will take a lot of abuse and holds up well over time.

“When choosing the correct weight for your kettlebell, it is key to consider your exercise,” says Almoni Ellis, CSCS, CPT. She says that people generally are able to use heavier weights when doing purely lower-body exercises, but that those weights may be too heavy for a person when they’re doing a move like an overhead press, for example.

Recent findings suggest that that said, there’s no one-size-fits-all starting point. Your experience level and current strength come into play, so if you’re unsure where to begin, try testing different weights at a local gym or consider ordering two sizes to see what feels best. As your strength improves, you can gradually increase the weight, adds Pack.

According to recent reports, the most common option for general strength training is the cast-iron kettlebell, which works well for everything from goblet squats to cleans to swings. These are the kettlebells you’ll most often see in home gyms and fitness classes.

It has been revealed that ellis and Pack recommend choosing a cast iron or steel kettlebell because they’re the most durable and long-lasting materials. “Kettlebells [that are] made up of plastic[...] don’t last as long,” Pack says.

According to recent reports, however, most adjustable kettlebells are made with some plastic components, which is necessary for the design. As for vinyl-coated kettlebells, they’re usually made of cast iron with a vinyl coating to prevent damage to floors.

Handle thickness plays a role in both comfort and performance. “Thicker handles can help build grip strength, but they may be more challenging for beginners to control,” claims Pack.

The handle’s coating and texture matter just as much. A slightly textured surface can help you maintain a secure grip, especially during dynamic or high-rep movements. Slick handles, on the other hand, can become slippery as your hands sweat—raising the risk of losing your grip, Pack adds. If you’re training with kettlebell that has a slick grip, consider using workout chalk or liquid chalk during moves like swings.

To choose the best kettlebells, I consulted three personal trainers who regularly work with kettlebells: Taylor Beebe, CPT, Tyneka Pack, CPT, and Almoni Ellis, CSCS. I also got feedback from Women’s Health fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT, who is a certified trainer.

Recent findings suggest that based on their feedback, I focused on crucial features to look for in these super versatile strength-training tools. I then tested some of the most popular kettlebells out there. Each was put through a slew of workouts to test its efficiency, durability, weight, material, and grip. Because every person’s budget is different, I made sure to include kettlebells with a range of price points.
